Reframed using the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS) lens: The FOMC’s hawkish hold at 5.25–5.50% is consistent with solid activity and modest disinflation, but SLOOS indicates tighter credit supply and softer loan demand that temper the positive tone and point to mounting headwinds.

SLOOS takeaways that lean the tone more cautious:
- Banks tightened lending standards and terms across C&I and consumer credit (credit cards, auto), including higher credit score requirements, lower loan sizes, tighter credit limits, and wider loan spreads—especially for riskier borrowers.
- CRE remains a focal stress: banks tightened standards broadly, lowered loan-to-value ratios, raised debt service coverage ratios, shortened interest-only periods, and narrowed market areas; demand for CRE credit remains weak.
- Weaker demand reported for C&I loans and several household loan categories, suggesting credit demand is cooling alongside supply constraints.
- Reasons cited include a more uncertain economic outlook, reduced risk tolerance, liquidity positions, industry-specific problems, supervisory and accounting considerations, and secondary market conditions.

Implication for the June 12 statement: While growth has been resilient and inflation is easing, SLOOS shows the higher-for-longer stance is transmitting through tighter bank credit and weaker loan demand, which should weigh on capex, consumer credit growth, and CRE. That combination argues for a more guarded interpretation of the outlook than a growth-only read would suggest.

Net: modestly positive on growth/disinflation progress, but credit-channel headwinds bring the tone close to neutral.
